comments.content: Template interpolation contains executable JavaScript, not literal text. For example, scanSource on `const s = `${1 /* Mark missing */}`;` reports the phrase inside the real block comment because this loop copies the entire template unchanged. This violates the requirement to ignore real comments and can make verify:wording reject compliant UI files. Track `${...}` expressions (including nested templates/braces) and strip comments inside those expressions; add a regression test.
comments.existing_code: while (j < source.length && source[j] !== c && (c === '`' || source[j] !== '\n')) j += source[j] === '\\' ? 2 : 1;

comments.content: Treating every apostrophe as a string opener still mishandles JSX text on the same line. For example, `const view = Don't; // Mark missing` produces a wording hit from the real trailing comment: the apostrophe causes the rest of the line to be copied without checking for comments. Ending at a newline only limits the damage; it does not preserve comment stripping for valid TSX. Distinguish JSX text from JavaScript string literals and cover this case with a regression test.

Handle escaped CRLF line continuations as a single escape. In a valid quoted string containing a backslash followed by CRLF, advancing by two skips only the backslash and CR, leaving LF to terminate this loop prematurely. For example, a source line `const a = 'x\` followed by CRLF and ` // '; const b = 'Mark missing';` incorrectly treats the literal's `//` as a comment and hides the prohibited phrase. Consume all three characters for a backslash-CRLF continuation so strings behave consistently with LF and CRLF files.
